**Move randomness into a parameter-independent input so the sampled value becomes a differentiable function.** For a Gaussian latent variable, draw epsilon from a standard normal and set $z=\mu+\sigma\epsilon$. Changes in mu shift the sample; changes in sigma stretch its displacement. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6114)

For fixed epsilon, the derivatives are straightforward: dz/dmu=1 and dz/dsigma=epsilon. Backpropagation can therefore differentiate a downstream reconstruction loss through z into the encoder's mean and scale outputs.

**Why ordinary sampling needs care.** Treating a sampled value as a constant misses how changing distribution parameters changes the expectation. Reparameterization provides a pathwise gradient estimator under conditions allowing differentiation and expectation to interchange.

A Monte Carlo sample still gives a noisy estimate, but it often has lower variance than a score-function estimator for suitable continuous distributions. Discrete samples generally need different estimators or relaxations, which introduce their own variance or bias. Stochastic computation is not inherently incompatible with gradients; the estimator must correctly account for the parameter-dependent distribution.

**Technical details and references.**

An ordinary sampling operation does not expose a deterministic differentiable path from its random output to distribution parameters. The gradient of an expectation also includes how the distribution changes; differentiating a fixed sampled value as a constant misses that dependence. For a Gaussian, sample parameter-independent $\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$ and set $z=\mu_\phi(x)+\sigma_\phi(x)\odot\epsilon$. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6114)

Now gradients pass through $\mu$ and $\sigma$ while averaging over fixed-noise draws: $\nabla_\phi\mathbb E_\epsilon f(z_\phi)=\mathbb E_\epsilon\nabla_\phi f(z_\phi)$ under suitable regularity. This is a pathwise estimator, often lower variance than a score-function estimator. It does not mean stochastic computation is inherently undifferentiable; it means the estimator must account for distributional dependence. Discrete sampling generally needs other estimators or relaxations, with their own bias/variance tradeoffs.
